rows.what the ink shows: A heavy continuous horizontal deletion covers almost the whole word. A short ascender survives near the first third and a descending-then-rising stroke near the right, but the intervening letter bodies have merged with the strike. The 4× contrast view and comparison with the unstruck word on the next line do not recover enough independent letters to certify the whole deleted word.

After the separate on, the word starts with an upright n/o join, then a tall t with a rightward crossbar, followed by low e-r strokes and a detached final a-shaped spot. The crossed t and the longer following run distinguish notera from voit.
The abbreviation has a long descending f stroke, a second high looped stroke for b, and a small lifted terminal l-t group. The same compact structure is separately visible in M0022 on this page.

After the deleted closing parenthesis, the first letter retains a tall d ascender and rounded foot below the crossing line; a small separate round o remnant follows, then a low connected n-c ending remains beneath the strike.

At the left of the deletion, the dotted i and tall l are visible, followed by the low e-s join and a t ascender. The middle word is almost completely merged into the thick deletion bar. At the right, a tall ascender and detached upper mark are compatible with the proposed déjà, but the remaining suffix cannot be securely separated into letters even in the 4× contrast view.

After sont, the ink again forms the long f descender, a high looped b stroke and a small raised terminal l-t curl. These are visibly the same abbreviated form as M0019, rather than a fully written adverb.

The first word has a tall looped b, a separate i dot and the low connected ending of bien. The next group visibly begins with a looped d, an upper acute mark and a crossed t. Its remaining letters flatten into a long run, followed by a small looped/ascending glyph; the 5× crop does not securely establish a separate car between the end of déterminé and the nearby mathematical a. The uncertainty therefore includes the two plausible word divisions.

The cramped margin group has a recognizable T top cap and long descending stem, together with two separate short oblique strokes identifiable as the double prime. The remaining descending/rounded marks are crowded against the right edge and do not reliably distinguish the parentheses and argument 1. A final 8× crop supports narrowing the uncertainty to that terminal part; the 5× and rotated views had not separated it.

The first character retains the broad top bar and vertical stem of a capital T. A following tall h-like stroke and low joined remnants survive, but the horizontal deletion covers the internal letters and any terminal abbreviation point. The 5× crop supports the T but does not establish every letter of herm.

The small overwritten glyph between Soit and the capital Gamma has an upper curved bowl and a lower hooked descender. The descending hook is consistent with the g forms actually visible in the two Gamma-g expressions on this page; no long upper crossbar belonging to a capital Gamma appears in the deleted glyph.

There is a capital T followed by a separate dot. The next group consists of a short e with an upper acute mark, a tall l stroke with a long baseline connector, and a small raised terminal t. There are no intervening ou-t letters or the longer letter sequence needed for fully written Tout élément.

Immediately after the large open C is a small compact rounded/triangular a with a short rightward exit. It has no pair of crossing diagonals; the following inclusion sign and capital R are separate. The visible ink therefore reads Ca, even though Cx might be expected from context.

After the opening parenthesis, the word begins with a descending p stroke, continues as a low u-i-s run with a distinct upper i dot, and ends in the long descending q/u connection and rightward e exit.
